name: Vector Index Internals
intent: See how approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (IVF, HNSW and product quantization) find close vectors without comparing with all of them, and which knobs trade recall for speed and memory.
scenario: A search feature must return the ten nearest of 100 million 768-dimensional vectors in a few milliseconds, on a budget that does not allow hundreds of gigabytes of memory.
problem: Exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query with every stored vector. That is N comparisons of d numbers each, and it is also the cost of holding all N vectors in memory at full precision. It is fine for thousands of vectors and hopeless for hundreds of millions. Every practical index gives up a little exactness: it looks only at the most promising candidates, and often stores compressed versions of the vectors. The skill is in knowing what each design gives up and which setting moves it.

howItWorks.title: Exact search is the baseline
howItWorks.text: Compare the query with every vector and keep the best k. It is always right and needs N x d multiply-adds per query. Full-precision vectors take N x d x 4 bytes: 100 million vectors of 768 numbers are about 307 GB. Exact search is also what you measure approximate indexes against.

howItWorks.title: IVF: search only the nearest cells
howItWorks.text: An inverted-file index runs k-means on the vectors to find C centroids and puts every vector in the list of its nearest centroid. A query is first compared with the C centroids, then only with the vectors in the nprobe closest lists. With about the square root of N lists, a query examines a small fraction of the data.

howItWorks.title: The cost of cells: boundaries
howItWorks.text: The true nearest neighbour can sit in a neighbouring cell whose centroid is not among the closest. Probing one list misses it, and probing more lists finds it at the price of more comparisons. The number of lists probed is the main recall against speed knob of an IVF index.

howItWorks.title: HNSW: walk a layered graph
howItWorks.text: A hierarchical navigable small world index links each vector to some of its near neighbours, in several layers. The top layers hold few vectors and make long jumps, and the bottom layer holds all of them. A search enters at the top, repeatedly moves to the neighbour closest to the query, drops down a layer, and continues. The paper reports much better logarithmic scaling than earlier graph methods. The graph links take memory on top of the vectors.

howItWorks.title: Product quantization shrinks the vectors
howItWorks.text: Product quantization splits each vector into m parts and replaces each part with the number of its nearest entry in a small codebook, one byte for 256 entries. A 128-number vector takes 512 bytes at full precision and 16 bytes with m = 16, which is 32 times less. Distances are estimated from the codes, and the method is typically combined with an inverted file.

howItWorks.title: Choose by measured recall
howItWorks.text: Recall is the share of the true nearest neighbours that the index returns. Measure it on sample queries against exact search, then pick the index and its settings for the recall you need within your latency and memory budget. Revisit it as data grows, since centroids and graphs built for old data can go stale.

pros: Query cost falls from the whole dataset to a small fraction of it
Product quantization cuts memory by an order of magnitude or more
The knobs (lists probed, search breadth) let one index serve different recall targets
Recall can be measured against exact search on a sample
cons: Results are approximate: the true nearest neighbour can be missed
Indexes must be built, and centroids or graphs can go stale as data changes
Graph indexes use extra memory for links, and compression loses some precision
Filters, updates and deletes are harder than in an exact scan
whenToUse: There are far more vectors than an exact scan can search within the latency budget
Memory is the limit, and compressed vectors can give acceptable recall
You can measure recall on real queries before choosing settings
whenNotToUse: Do not build an approximate index for a collection small enough to scan exactly
Do not choose settings by speed alone, without measuring the recall they give
Do not assume an index built last year suits data that has changed a lot
pitfalls: Measuring latency but not recall, and shipping an index that misses many true neighbours
Compressing vectors without checking how much it hurts the results for your queries
Forgetting that adding a metadata filter can leave an index with too few matching candidates
Treating an index as static when new vectors keep arriving and their distribution drifts

roles.label: Query vector
roles.description: The embedding of the question, for which the nearest stored vectors are wanted.

roles.label: Index structure
roles.description: Centroids and lists (IVF) or a layered graph (HNSW) that narrows the search.

roles.label: Candidates
roles.description: The small set of vectors that are actually compared with the query.

roles.label: Compressed codes
roles.description: Short codes (product quantization) that replace full-precision vectors to save memory.

quiz.question: An IVF index probing a single list sometimes returns a result that is not the true nearest neighbour. What is the cause, and the fix?
options: The index is corrupted, so it must be rebuilt from scratch each time this is noticed
The true neighbour sat in a neighbouring list, so probing more lists finds it at the price of more comparisons
The vectors are too short, so they should be padded with zeros to make the index accurate
The query was compared with too many centroids, so reduce the number of lists to make it stricter
quiz.explanation: A vector near a cell boundary can be closer to a query than anything in the query's own cell. Raising the number of lists probed reduces that risk and costs more work. The index is not corrupted, padding does not help, and fewer lists make cells larger and the search more expensive.

quiz.question: A team has 100 million 768-dimensional float32 vectors, about 307 GB, and 30 GB of memory for them. Which technique cuts memory the most?
options: Raising the number of lists probed, which makes each stored vector smaller
Using a graph index, because graphs store each vector in fewer bytes than a list does
Increasing the dimensions of the vectors, so that each one carries more information
Product quantization, which replaces each vector with a short code of a few bytes
quiz.explanation: Product quantization stores a short code per vector, for example 16 bytes instead of 3072, and that is what brings the total within a memory budget. The number of lists probed does not change storage, graph indexes add link memory, and larger vectors need more.

quiz.question: Which description best matches how an HNSW index answers a query?
options: It starts in a sparse top layer, moves to the neighbour closest to the query, then drops to denser layers and repeats
It sorts all vectors by the first coordinate and scans the ones whose value is closest to the query's
It hashes the query to a bucket and returns everything in that bucket without any further comparison
It compares the query with every vector, but does so in parallel on many threads at the same time
quiz.explanation: HNSW is a layered proximity graph: long jumps in the sparse upper layers get close quickly, and the dense bottom layer refines the answer. Sorting by one coordinate, a single bucket and a parallel full scan are not how it works.
